claim: MESNa treatment can remove over 99.9% of biotin from cells labelled with sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin at 4°C.
source: MESNa treatment could remove over 99.9% of biotin from cells labelled at 4°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating serial dilution and detection of biotin after MESNa treatment.

claim: Washes at pH3 remove up to 50% of antibody bound to the GPI-anchored protein CD59.
source: Washes at pH3 to remove bound antibody, or PI-PLC to cleave GPI-anchors, were around two orders of magnitude less efficient, removing up to 50% and 90% of antibody bound to the GPI-anchored protein CD59 respectively (Figure 1B) (Davies et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing efficiency of different methods for removing surface-bound antibody.

claim: PI-PLC treatment removes up to 90% of antibody bound to the GPI-anchored protein CD59.
source: Washes at pH3 to remove bound antibody, or PI-PLC to cleave GPI-anchors, were around two orders of magnitude less efficient, removing up to 50% and 90% of antibody bound to the GPI-anchored protein CD59 respectively (Figure 1B) (Davies et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating PI-PLC cleavage efficiency.

claim: Reducible biotin and MESNa offer a highly accurate way of assaying protein internalisation.
source: Reducible biotin and MESNa therefore offer a highly accurate way of assaying protein internalisation.
evidence: Based on inference from the comparative efficiency data showing MESNa removes >99.9% of biotin versus 50-90% for other methods.

claim: Endocytic vesicles can be observed after as little as 20 s of internalisation using the sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin method.
source: Endocytic vesicles could be observed after as little as 20 s of internalisation.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Surface biotinylation with sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin labels a wide range of plasma membrane proteins including rare proteins with estimated copy number < 100 per cell.
source: Abundant plasma membrane proteins had higher chances of being detected. Nevertheless, a wide range of rare proteins (some with estimated copy number < 100 per cell) was detected, assuring us that we achieved good coverage of the total plasma membrane protein complement. (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS data comparing detected proteins with quantitative proteome analysis, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Over 95% of the total internalised biotin after 20 s uptake is present in transferrin-positive vesicles.
source: This revealed that over 95% of the total internalised biotin after 20 s uptake was present in transferrin-positive vesicles (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of co-localization between biotin and transferrin shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After 20 s uptake over 80% of biotin-positive endocytic vesicles co-localise with clathrin in small puncta.
source: Additionally, after 20 s uptake over 80% of biotin-positive endocytic vesicles co-localised with clathrin in small puncta, defining them as clathrin-coated vesicles (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The proportion of biotin-positive vesicles co-localising with clathrin falls rapidly with longer periods of uptake.
source: The proportion co-localising with clathrin fell rapidly with longer periods of uptake, as one would expect due to uncoating of primary vesicles (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5) (Kirchhausen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by time-course data in Figure 2D and cited literature on clathrin uncoating.

claim: Approximately 2% of cells contain distinctively larger macropinosomes over 500 nm in diameter.
source: Approximately 2% of the cells also contained distinctively larger macropinosomes over 500 nm in diameter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large, fluid-filled macropinosomes are completely devoid of transferrin.
source: Uptake of transferrin was solely due to binding to transferrin receptor, as large, fluid-filled macropinosomes were completely devoid of transferrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing macropinosomes without transferrin signal.

claim: Co-localisation between internalised biotin and transferrin remains constant when times of internalisation up to 150 s are assayed.
source: Co-localisation remained constant when times of internalisation up to 150 s were assayed (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B across multiple time points.

claim: Nearly all of the internalised protein labelled with biotin is present in transferrin-positive vesicles when labelling is carried out at 37°C.
source: Consistent with the results when labelling was carried out at 4°C, nearly all of the internalised protein labelled with biotin was indeed present in transferrin-positive vesicles (Figure 2E, Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and 2F using continuous labeling at 37°C.

claim: There is near-complete co-localisation between endocytosed sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin and transferrin after 90 s uptake at 37°C in Cos7 and RPE cells.
source: Again, there was near-complete co-localisation between endocytosed sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin and transferrin after 90 s uptake at 37°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 from experiments in Cos7 and RPE cells.

claim: 90% of the FM1-43FX signal present in intracellular vesicles is also present in transferrin-positive pixels.
source: Quantification revealed that 90% of the FM1-43FX signal present in intracellular vesicles was also present in transferrin-positive pixels (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: After 90 s continuous labelling and uptake 96% of 2350 vesicles contained transferrin.
source: Applying this conservative criterion, after 90 s continuous labelling and uptake 96% of 2350 vesicles contained transferrin, and after labelling at 4°C and uptake for 20 s 92% of 2387 vesicles contained transferrin (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by 3D object-based quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After labelling at 4°C and uptake for 20 s, 92% of 2387 vesicles contained transferrin.
source: Applying this conservative criterion, after 90 s continuous labelling and uptake 96% of 2350 vesicles contained transferrin, and after labelling at 4°C and uptake for 20 s 92% of 2387 vesicles contained transferrin (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by 3D object-based quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A single Gaussian curve can describe the transferrin intensity distribution within most identified vesicles.
source: A single Gaussian curve could describe the transferrin intensity distribution within most identified vesicles, consistent with stochastic incorporation of transferrin receptors into forming clathrin-coated pits (Collinet et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by analysis of transferrin intensity distributions and cited literature on stochastic cargo incorporation.

claim: There is no correlation between biotin intensity and the probability of a vesicle not containing transferrin.
source: We observed no correlation between biotin intensity and the probability of that vesicle not containing transferrin, arguing against the possibility of a morphologically distinctive class of transferrin-negative endocytic vesicle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The transferrin load in vesicles in control and CTB treated cells is the same.
source: The transferrin load in vesicles in control and CTB treated cells was the same (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cells overexpressing AP180-C, transferrin uptake and endocytosis of total biotinylated protein are both efficiently blocked, with total protein uptake being reduced to less than 5% of control levels.
source: In cells overexpressing AP180-C, transferrin uptake and endocytosis of total biotinylated protein were both efficiently blocked, with total protein uptake being reduced to less than 5% of control levels (Figure 3C and Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C and 3E from AP180-C overexpression experiments.

claim: In cells overexpressing dynamin 2 K44A there is efficient reduction of both transferrin and total biotinylated protein uptake to less than 5% of control levels.
source: In cells overexpressing dynamin 2 K44A there was efficient reduction of both transferrin and total biotinylated protein uptake to less than 5% of control levels (Figure 3D and Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D and 3F from dynamin 2 K44A overexpression experiments.

claim: Expression of very high levels of dynamin 2 K44A induces endocytosis of total biotinylated protein in both macropinosomes and smaller vesicular structures.
source: Additionally, we noted that expression of very high levels of the dynamin mutant induced endocytosis of total biotinylated protein in both macropinosomes and smaller vesicular structures (see below).
evidence: Supported by observations described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AP2 siRNA blocks alpha-adaptin expression and hence AP2 function.
source: In order to ablate coated pit activity, cells were transfected with siRNA against the alpha adaptin subunit of the clathrin adaptor AP2 ('AP2 siRNA'). This blocked alpha-adaptin expression, and hence AP2 function (Figure 4A, Figure 4B) (Motley et al., 2003, 2006).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A and cited literature on AP2 function.

claim: AP2 siRNA blocks both transferrin uptake and uptake of total biotinylated proteins to a similar extent.
source: AP2 siRNA blocked both transferrin uptake and uptake of total biotinylated proteins to a similar extent (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AP2 siRNA treatment causes a clear and pronounced increase in the abundance of most plasma membrane proteins.
source: This revealed a clear and pronounced increase in the abundance of most proteins in AP2-siRNA cells (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SILAC ratios of non-biotinylated cytosolic proteins do not reveal similar changes to plasma membrane proteins after AP2 depletion.
source: Analysis of SILAC ratios of the non-biotinylated cytosolic proteins present in the flow-through provided an internal control and did not reveal similar changes, confirming that the effects of AP2 depletion are largely restricted to the population of plasma membrane proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by SILAC analysis shown in Figure 4C comparing biotinylated and non-biotinylated protein populations.

claim: Most GPI-anchored proteins detected are depleted from the plasma membrane upon AP2 siRNA treatment.
source: The only obvious pattern within the list is the presence of most GPI-anchored proteins detected (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 4D highlighting GPI-anchored proteins.

claim: AP2 siRNA causes an accumulation of transferrin receptor at the plasma membrane.
source: Flow cytometry to assay changes in plasma membrane levels of individual proteins confirmed that AP2 siRNA causes an accumulation of transferrin receptor at the plasma membrane, while levels of the GPI-anchored protein CD59 are reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AP2 siRNA causes levels of the GPI-anchored protein CD59 at the plasma membrane to be reduced.
source: Flow cytometry to assay changes in plasma membrane levels of individual proteins confirmed that AP2 siRNA causes an accumulation of transferrin receptor at the plasma membrane, while levels of the GPI-anchored protein CD59 are reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All four GPI-anchored proteins (CD59, folate receptor, PrP, and minimal SNAP-GPI) co-localise extensively with transferrin after internalisation.
source: All four GPI-anchored proteins co-localised extensively with transferrin after internalisation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Around 90% of all BG-SS-488 labelled, internalised GPI-anchored proteins co-localise with transferrin.
source: When quantified, around 90% of all BG-SS-488 labelled, internalised GPI-anchored proteins co-localised with transferrin (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Around 90% co-localisation is detected between transferrin-alexa-647 and transferrin-alexa-546 after simultaneous internalisation.
source: To assess the biological significance of the residual 10% we used precisely the same quantification method to analyse co-localisation between transferrin-alexa-647 and transferrin-alexa-546, after mixing and adding to cells for simultaneous internalisation. Again we detected around 90% co-localisation, so it is possible that the residual 10% can be accounted for by limitations in quantification rather than a biologically significant pool of GPI-anchored protein internalised separately from transferrin (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CTB-binding does not alter the proportion of vesicles that are potentially transferrin-negative in cells expressing SNAP-CD59.
source: The proportion of vesicles that are potentially transferrin-negative (the fraction below the dotted line) is not altered by CTB-binding.
evidence: Supported by object-based analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SS-atto-488 signal from doubly labelled anti-CD59 antibody co-localises completely with transferrin after 90s uptake.
source: The SS-atto-488 signal co-localised completely with transferrin.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A using doubly-labeled antibody.

claim: Alexa-546 from doubly labelled anti-CD59 antibody is seen in many punctate structures that lack transferrin after PI-PLC treatment.
source: Alexa-546, however, was seen in many punctate structures that lack transferrin (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PI-PLC treatment does not remove all external GPI-anchored protein.
source: We interpret these data as strong evidence that the PI-PLC treatment did not remove all external GPI-anchored protein, while reduction with MESNa provided more stringent discrimination between internal and external pools of the antibody (Figure 1A, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of MESNa and PI-PLC efficiency data.

claim: Endogenous CD59 is internalised in transferrin-containing vesicles.
source: Therefore, endogenous CD59 is indeed internalised in transferrin-containing vesicles, and apparent internalisation in vesicles lacking transferrin may, at least under the conditions we have employed in this study, be an artifact due to incomplete removal of surface bound antibody.
evidence: Based on inference from the doubly-labeled antibody experiment results.

claim: In cells expressing AP180-C, endocytosis of SNAP-CD59 is blocked to the same extent as endocytosis of transferrin.
source: In cells expressing AP180-C, endocytosis of SNAP-CD59 was blocked to the same extent as endocytosis of transferrin (Figure 6B and Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: Endocytosis of SNAP-CD59 is blocked by moderate expression of dynamin-2-K44A.
source: Endocytosis of SNAP-CD59 was also blocked by moderate expression of dynamin-2-K44A (Figure 6C and Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C and 6E.

claim: In cells expressing very high levels of dynamin-2-K44A, abundant macropinosomes and smaller endocytic structures can be detected.
source: In cells expressing very high levels of the mutant dynamin, abundant macropinosomes could be detected, as well as smaller endocytic structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Damke et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Around 2% of caveolin 1 is present specifically in biotin-positive endosomes after both 90 s and 15 min.
source: In the case of caveolin 1, after both 90 s and 15 min some apparent co-localisation in punctate structures could be observed, and quantification confirmed that around 2% of caveolin 1 was present specifically in biotin-positive endosomes (Figure 7A, Figure 7B, 15 min time-point images in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Flotillin 1 co-localisation with internalised biotin may arise purely by chance.
source: In the case of flotillin 1, although some plausible co-localisation could be observed in confocal images, quantification revealed that this may arise purely by chance as the same degree of pixel overlap was found in offset and original images (Figure 7C, Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with offset controls shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Internalised biotin is detected in GRAF1-GFP-positive puncta.
source: In the case of GRAF1, internalised biotin was detected in GRAF1-GFP-positive puncta (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 7E.

claim: GRAF1-positive endosomes contain transferrin.
source: The fact that our previous data show that most internalised biotin/total protein co-localises with transferrin made the strong prediction that these GRAF1-positive endosomes should also contain transferrin. This was indeed the case (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by three-color microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ARF6 labels transferrin-positive endosomes.
source: ARF6 showed a similar distribution to GRAF1, labelling transferrin-positive endosomes (Figure 7G, Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claim: GRAF1-GFP and ARF6-GFP are present on transferrin-positive endocytic vesicles likely to have arisen from budding of clathrin-coated pits from the plasma membrane.
source: We conclude that GRAF1-GFP and ARF6-GFP are present on transferrin-positive endocytic vesicles likely to have arisen from budding of clathrin-coated pits from the plasma membrane, that flotillin 1 is not detected on early endosomes, and that caveolin 1 is present on a very small fraction of endosomes.
evidence: Based on inference from co-localization data with transferrin and biotin.

claim: Flotillin 1 is not detected on early endosomes.
source: We conclude that GRAF1-GFP and ARF6-GFP are present on transferrin-positive endocytic vesicles likely to have arisen from budding of clathrin-coated pits from the plasma membrane, that flotillin 1 is not detected on early endosomes, and that caveolin 1 is present on a very small fraction of endosomes.
evidence: Based on inference from co-localization data showing no specific overlap above background.

claim: Caveolin 1 is present on a very small fraction of endosomes.
source: We conclude that GRAF1-GFP and ARF6-GFP are present on transferrin-positive endocytic vesicles likely to have arisen from budding of clathrin-coated pits from the plasma membrane, that flotillin 1 is not detected on early endosomes, and that caveolin 1 is present on a very small fraction of endosomes.
evidence: Based on quantitative data showing ~2% co-localization.

claim: AP2 siRNA causes a more pronounced reduction of transferrin uptake than CD59 uptake.
source: AP2 siRNA caused a more pronounced reduction of transferrin than CD59 uptake.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A comparing ratios of transferrin to CD59 uptake.

claim: Transferrin uptake is more sensitive to reduction of AP2 levels than uptake of SNAP-CD59.
source: The uptake of both cargoes was efficiently blocked when AP2 levels became close to zero, but transferrin uptake was clearly more sensitive to reduction of AP2 levels than uptake of SNAP-CD59. (Figure 8C; see also Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Overexpression of µ2(F174S/D176A) causes a dramatic differential effect on the uptake of transferrin and SNAP-CD59 after 90 s of labelling and internalisation.
source: Overexpression of µ2(F174S/D176A), but not wild-type μ2, caused a dramatic differential effect on the uptake of the two cargoes after 90 s of labelling and internalisation.
evidence: Supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 8D-G.

claim: Overexpression of µ2(F174S/D176A) reduces transferrin uptake.
source: As predicted, transferrin uptake was reduced (Honing et al., 2005, Motley et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8G and cited literature.

claim: Overexpression of µ2(F174S/D176A) significantly increases uptake of SNAP-CD59.
source: Uptake of SNAP-CD59, however, was significantly increased (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Internalised SNAP-CD59 co-localises with residual internalised transferrin in cells expressing µ2(F174S/D176A).
source: Importantly, this divergence did not arise from separate endocytic structures, as internalised SNAP-CD59 still co-localised well with the residual internalised transferrin (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: There is a clear increase in the SNAP-CD59 load in transferrin-positive vesicles in cells expressing µ2(F174S/D176A).
source: Moreover, when 3D object-based analysis was used to identify transferrin-positive vesicles, and to quantify the amount of SNAP-CD59 present in these vesicles, a clear increase in the SNAP-CD59 load in mutant-expressing cells was observed (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by 3D object-based quantification shown in Figure 8F.

claim: There is reduced transferrin load in endocytic vesicles in cells expressing µ2(F174S/D176A).
source: This analysis also confirmed the reduced transferrin load in endocytic vesicles in mutant-expressing cells (Figure 8G).
evidence: Supported by 3D object-based quantification shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Steric exclusion of GPI-anchored proteins from the nascent pit becomes less acute when recruitment of high-affinity cargoes by AP2 is abolished.
source: These results are in agreement with our initial hypothesis of distinctive sorting of GPI-anchored proteins into clathrin coated pits. They argue that steric exclusion of GPI-anchored proteins from the nascent pit becomes less acute when recruitment of high-affinity cargoes by AP2, or potentially other adaptors is abolished (Bhagatji et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on inference from the differential effects observed with the µ2 mutant and cited literature.

claim: Rates of endocytosis of high affinity cargoes may be more susceptible to perturbations of coated pit function than cargoes like GPI-anchored proteins, which have a lower affinity for the nascent pit.
source: More generally, the data imply that rates of endocytosis of high affinity cargoes may be more susceptible to a range of perturbations of coated pit function than cargoes like GPI-anchored proteins, which have a lower affinity for the nascent pit.
evidence: Based on inference from the differential sensitivity to AP2 depletion and mutation.

claim: At least 95% of the earliest detectable endocytic vesicles arise from clathrin-coated pits.
source: We find that at least 95% of the earliest detectable endocytic vesicles arise from clathrin-coated pits.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental data including co-localization with transferrin and clathrin.

claim: GPI-anchored proteins enter the cell predominantly via coated pits.
source: GPI-anchored proteins, candidate cargoes for alternate pathways, are also found to enter the cell predominantly via coated pits.
evidence: Supported by co-localization data with transferrin and perturbation experiments.

claim: The predominant pathway for endocytosis in mammalian cells, accounting for at least 95% of total protein endocytic flux, is uptake via the clathrin-coated pit.
source: Our data support the conclusions that the predominant pathway for endocytosis in mammalian cells, accounting for at least 95% of total protein endocytic flux, is uptake via the clathrin-coated pit.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of endocytic vesicles using multiple methods.

claim: Other endocytic mechanisms are not likely to make a significant contribution to total endocytic flux.
source: Other mechanisms are not likely to make a significant contribution.
evidence: Based on inference from the finding that >95% of endocytosis occurs via clathrin-coated pits.

claim: Primary endocytic vesicles involved in clathrin-independent endocytosis should not contain significant amounts of transferrin receptor.
source: Primary endocytic vesicles involved in clathrin-independent endocytosis should not contain significant amounts of transferrin receptor, and while we can detect a class of such vesicles they account for less than 5% of total endocytosis.
evidence: Based on logical inference about what would define clathrin-independent vesicles and quantitative data.

claim: A class of vesicles that do not contain significant amounts of transferrin receptor can be detected and they account for less than 5% of total endocytosis.
source: Primary endocytic vesicles involved in clathrin-independent endocytosis should not contain significant amounts of transferrin receptor, and while we can detect a class of such vesicles they account for less than 5% of total endocytosis.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of transferrin content in endocytic vesicles.

claim: Clathrin-independent pathways do not make a significant contribution to total endocytic flux in cultured cells.
source: Nevertheless, we conclude that clathrin-independent pathways do not make a significant contribution to total endocytic flux in cultured cells.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis showing >95% of endocytosis occurs via clathrin-coated pits.

claim: Clathrin-independent endocytic pathways could still be functionally important when uptake of specific cargoes and the variety of cell types and functions in vivo are considered.
source: Such clathrin-independent pathways could still be functionally important when uptake of specific cargoes, and the variety of cell types and functions in vivo are considered (Commisso et al., 2013; Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative statement acknowledging potential importance in specific contexts, supported by citations.

claim: GPI-anchored proteins are partially excluded from coated pits by steric crowding effects.
source: It is likely that GPI-anchored proteins are partially excluded from coated pits by steric crowding effects (Bhagatji et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of cytosolic domain and cited literature.

claim: The mutant µ2(F174S/D176A) used in this study was previously incorrectly described in publications due to a typographic error.
source: A typographic error for the YXXΦ binding mutant is present in previous publications (Honing et al., 2005; Edeling et al., 2006; Motley et al., 2006). The mutant used and characterised in those studies was as described here (David Owen, personal communication).
evidence: Based on personal communication clarifying previous publications.

claim: The µ2(F174S/D176A) mutant incorporates into endogenous AP2 complexes after overexpression.
source: Overexpression of this mutant form of μ2 for 4 days resulted in incorporation into endogenous AP2 complexes, and thereby provided a tool to further investigate sorting of transferrin and GPI-anchored proteins into coated pits (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.
